about.html.main_text: Home/About Josh About Josh Your local tech guy. Minus the tech-speak. I’m Josh Sargent—the person behind The Tech Tamer. I help people and small businesses across Eastern Iowa get more comfortable with their technology. Howdy there! When your tech won’t cooperate, I’m the guy you call. I’ve been helping people work through technology problems since I was a kid in the ’90s. What started as helping family and friends grew into The Tech Tamer: practical, personal help for the things you use every day. I’m no plumber. When a pipe leaks, I call someone who knows what they’re doing. Technology is my version of that—I’m here to help when a device won’t cooperate or you don’t know where to start. Sometimes that means getting a printer connected. Sometimes it means setting up a TV, making a phone less confusing, or helping a small business bring its branding and technology together. Whatever the project, you’ll work directly with me. I’ll explain the plan in plain English and help you understand what comes next. scam-help.html.main_text: Home/Scam & hacked-account help Scam & account help · Muscatine, Iowa Scam & Hacked Account Help in Muscatine A pop-up says your computer is infected. Someone’s posting from your Facebook. You can’t get into your email. Take a breath. It happens to smart, careful people every day, and you don’t have to sort it out alone. I’m Josh, and I’ll help you get back in and lock things down. Text Josh↗Call 563-261-0200↗ Evenings & weekends: Sun–Tue & Thu–Sat, 8 AM–8 PM. Wednesday: appointment setting only. Right now, before anything else Think you’ve been scammed or hacked? Take a breath. Here’s what to do. First, it’s not your fault. Scammers are professionals, and they work hard to make things feel urgent. You don’t have to fix everything this minute. Go through these steps in order, at your own pace. They’re safe to do on your own while you wait to hear back from me. 1 Stop. Don’t pay or send anything more. If someone is rushing you to pay, buy gift cards or move money, stop there. A real company will wait while you check. 2 Hang up or close the pop-up. Don’t call the number. Close the browser. If a warning won’t go away, hold the power button to turn the computer off. Real companies don’t put phone numbers in warning pop-ups. 3 Don’t give out codes or remote access. Never read back a code sent to your phone, and don’t let anyone connect to your computer, no matter who they say they are. 4 From a safe device, change your passwords. Start with email. Use a phone or computer you trust. Your email comes first, because it can reset almost everything else. 5 Turn on 2-step verification. Add it to your email, bank and social accounts, so a stolen password alone isn’t enough to get in. 6 Call your bank if money or a card was involved. Use the number on the back of your card, not a number from a message or a caller. 7 Save screenshots and details. Write down names, phone numbers, times and amounts, and take screenshots. They help your bank, and they help when you report it. 8 Check for remote-access software. If you let someone connect to your computer, keep it off the internet until it’s checked for programs they may have left behind. I can check it with you. Still worried, or need a hand with this? Reach out to me. Text or call 563-261-0200. Tell me what happened in your own words. No judgment, and no rushing. Text Josh↗Call 563-261-0200↗ The free guide: jump to a section What to do right now Spot common scams Signs an account was hacked Lock your accounts down Protect older family members Where to report it Quick answers How to spot them Common scams, and what they look like. Most scams follow the same few scripts. Once you know them, they get a lot easier to recognize. Fake “virus” pop-ups A full-screen warning, sometimes with an alarm sound, says your computer is infected and gives a phone number to call. Microsoft, Apple and Google don’t put phone numbers in warnings like that. Close the browser, or hold the power button if it won’t close. Tech-support calls Someone calls saying they’re from Microsoft, Apple, Amazon or your internet company, and that your computer has a problem. Real companies don’t call you out of the blue about a virus. Hang up. If you’re unsure, call the company yourself at a number you look up. Bank, Amazon and delivery texts “Unusual charge on your account.” “Your package can’t be delivered.” “Your account is locked.” Don’t tap the link. Open the company’s own app, or call the number on the back of your card, and check from there. Gift cards and odd payments No real business, utility or government office asks you to pay with gift cards, a wire transfer, cryptocurrency or a payment app to a stranger. If anyone asks you to read off the numbers on the back of a gift card, it’s a scam. Grandparent and family emergencies “Grandma, it’s me. I’m in trouble. Please don’t tell Mom.” Sometimes a “lawyer” or “officer” gets on the line. Voices can be faked now. Hang up and call your family member at the number you already have for them. Romance and too-good-to-be-true A new online friend who can never meet in person and soon has a money problem. A prize you have to pay to collect. An investment that “can’t lose.” Sending money to someone you’ve never met, or paying to win, is your cue to stop. The four big red flags. Pressure (act right now), secrecy (don’t tell anyone, stay on the line), strange payment (gift cards, wire, crypto) and access (codes, passwords, remote control of your computer). Any one of them is reason enough to stop and check with someone you trust. Is it hacked? Signs an account was hacked. Not sure if someone got into your account? These are the usual clues. Friends say they got strange messages or friend requests from you. Your password suddenly stops working. You get emails or texts about sign-ins, password changes or new devices that weren’t you. There are sent emails, posts or purchases you didn’t make. Your recovery phone number or backup email has been changed. Sign-in codes arrive that you didn’t ask for. Seeing one of these? Start with your email, from a phone or computer you trust. Change the password, then turn on 2-step verification. The checklist at the top walks through the order. If a sign-in code shows up that you didn’t ask for, don’t share it with anyone. It usually means someone has your password, so change it. Lock it down Lock your accounts down. A few settings make the next scam a lot harder to pull off. Start with your email, then your bank, then everything else. Password manager basics Use a different password for every account, so one leak doesn’t open the rest. A password manager remembers them for you. One is built into iPhones, Android phones and the Chrome browser. A notebook kept safe at home is better than reusing the same password everywhere. 2-step verification This adds a second check, like a code sent to your phone or a tap on an approval prompt, when someone signs in. A stolen password alone isn’t enough anymore. Turn it on for email first. Never read that code to anyone who calls or texts you. Recovery info Make sure each important account has a current recovery phone number and backup email. That’s how you get back in if you’re ever locked out. Check them once a year, and any time you change phone numbers. For the person everyone calls Protect older family members. Scammers often target older adults. A little planning together goes a long way, and it works best without a lecture. Talk about it, kindly Share the common scripts above, like the fake pop-up and the “grandchild in trouble” call, so they’re easy to spot. Make it a conversation, not a test. Make a “call me first” rule Agree that before anyone sends money, buys gift cards or lets someone onto the computer, they call you (or me) first. A real request can wait five minutes. Pick a family code word A word only your family knows. If a caller claims to be a grandchild in trouble and can’t give it, hang up and call that grandchild directly. Save the numbers that matter Put the bank, family members and a trusted helper in their phone contacts, so they don’t have to search for numbers under pressure. Turn on call and spam filters Most phones and carriers can silence unknown callers or flag likely spam. With their permission, help set up 2-step verification and recovery info too. No shame if it happens If they get fooled, thank them for telling you. People who feel embarrassed stop asking for help, and that’s exactly what scammers want. Report it Where to report a scam. Reporting helps warn others and creates a record. It doesn’t always get money back, so if money or a card was involved, call your bank first. Your bank or card company Call the number on the back of your card, not a number from a text, email or caller. Tell them what happened and ask what they can do. ReportFraud.ftc.gov The Federal Trade Commission collects reports on scams and fraud. ReportFraud.ftc.gov ↗ IdentityTheft.gov If someone used your name, Social Security number or opened accounts as you, this FTC site gives you a step-by-step plan. IdentityTheft.gov ↗ FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center For scams that happened online, especially if money was lost. ic3.gov ↗ Good questions Scam help: the quick answers. A pop-up says my computer is infected and gives a phone number. Should I call? No. Real companies like Microsoft and Apple don’t put phone numbers in warning pop-ups. Don’t call, don’t let anyone connect to your computer, and don’t pay. Close the browser, or turn the computer off if it won’t close, and text me. I already let someone onto my computer. What now? Don’t panic. Turn the computer off or disconnect it from the internet. If you shared banking details or paid anything, call your bank using the number on the back of your card. Then call me, and we’ll check the computer and change the passwords that matter, from a safe device. Can you get my hacked account back? I’ll work through every recovery option the company offers with you, step by step. I can’t promise every account can be recovered, because that decision is up to the company. If there’s a way back in, we’ll find it together. What does scam help cost? The same as any tech help: $50 an hour, and the first conversation is free. On-site visits have a one-hour minimum. I’ll never ask you for gift cards. How do I keep this from happening again? Turn on 2-step verification for your email and important accounts, use a different password for each one, and pause before you click. The lock-it-down tips and family tips on this page walk you through it. Need help right now? Call or text Josh at 563-261-0200. Evenings & weekends: Sun–Tue & Thu–Sat, 8 AM–8 PM. Wednesday: appointment setting only. Text Josh↗Call Josh↗ Need other tech help? See tech help in Muscatine or the areas I serve. Worried about a scam? Let’s check it together.
